cards.title: The Context Map: Naming What Exists
cards.teaser: A context map is not a wishful architecture diagram — it is a brutally honest picture of the relationships that already exist between bounded contexts: who depends on whom, who sets terms, and who absorbs change.

runs.text: In Domain-Driven Design, a
context map

documents the relationships between bounded contexts across a system. Eric Evans introduced it in the blue book as a way to make the political and technical reality of multi-context systems legible. The map does not prescribe the ideal state — it names the current state so teams can reason about it and improve it.

Without a context map, integration patterns accumulate silently. One team calls another team's endpoints without a clear integration contract. A downstream team copies an upstream model into their own codebase and the copies drift apart. A third team rewrites a service and breaks four unknown consumers. These are context-map problems that went unmanaged.
A context map answers three questions for every inter-context relationship:

items.text: Who is upstream and who is downstream?
The upstream team's model changes flow downstream. The downstream team absorbs or translates those changes.
What is the integration pattern?
Shared kernel, conformist, ACL, OHS — each pattern has different coordination costs and coupling characteristics.
What is the team relationship?
Partnership, customer-supplier, or no relationship at all? The team relationship determines whether the downstream team can influence the upstream model.

runs.text: Drawing a context map is often the most politically charged act in a DDD initiative — because it makes visible who holds power over whom in the codebase.
Evans's original guidance: draw the map on a whiteboard with the whole team. Include team names, not just system names. The team boundaries matter as much as the code boundaries.
A context map is a diagram of who talks to whom, on whose terms, and who has to change when something breaks. It names the reality that teams usually feel but never write down.

cards.title: Drawing a Context Map: Conventions
cards.teaser: Context maps use a small vocabulary of boxes, arrows, and labels. The conventions are loose by DDD standards — what matters is legibility, not formal notation. A hand-drawn map on a whiteboard beats a UML diagram nobody updates.

runs.text: There is no single mandated notation for context maps. The community has converged on a minimal set of conventions that are expressive enough to capture relationships without requiring a modeling tool.
The basic notation:

items.text: Boxes (or named ovals)
represent bounded contexts. Include both the context name and the owning team name inside the box.
Arrows
represent data/model flow. Arrow direction = information flows from upstream to downstream. Arrowheads point at the downstream context.
Labels on the arrow
name the relationship pattern:
ACL
CF
(conformist),
OHS
PL
(published language),
SK
(shared kernel),
CS
(customer-supplier).
U and D markers
placed on each end of an arrow indicate the upstream (U) and downstream (D) side.

runs.text: An ASCII context map showing common patterns:

Keep the map at the team level, not the service level. A context map with 40 boxes is a micro-services deployment diagram, not a DDD context map. If you have more than 10-12 contexts on a single map, consider drawing cluster maps that zoom into specific regions.
Draw boxes for contexts (with team names), draw arrows from upstream to downstream, and label each arrow with the relationship type. That is the whole notation. It fits on a whiteboard.

cards.title: Upstream and Downstream: The Power Dynamic
cards.teaser: Every integration has an upstream and a downstream. The upstream team decides what the model looks like. The downstream team has to live with that decision. Understanding who holds that power is the foundation of every integration pattern in DDD.

runs.text: The upstream/downstream distinction is not technical — it is organizational. The
upstream
context is the one whose model or API changes flow outward to other contexts. Changes to the upstream model ripple to everyone downstream. The
downstream
context is the one that must adapt to those changes.
Power asymmetry is the core tension the integration patterns manage:

items.text: High-power upstream:
An external SaaS provider (Stripe, Salesforce, Twilio) or a platform team with many consumers. They set the contract; you adapt. They have no incentive to accommodate your model.
Balanced upstream:
An internal team where both sides negotiate the contract. The downstream team has a seat at the table. Customer-supplier and partnership patterns live here.
Weak upstream:
A legacy system that nobody actively maintains. It changes unpredictably (or not at all), and no team is responsible for its consumers. This is the ACL use case.

runs.text: The direction of the arrow on a context map is not about data volume or call frequency. It is about whose model dominates. A downstream context that calls an upstream API ten thousand times per second is still downstream — it has to conform to the upstream's schema.

Failing to identify the power dynamic leads to integration bugs that look technical but are organizational. A team assumes they can rename an upstream field; the upstream team has no idea the downstream team exists. The rename ships; the downstream breaks. A context map would have surfaced this dependency before the rename.

Upstream is whoever controls the model. Downstream is whoever has to live with whatever upstream decides. All eight integration patterns are different answers to the same question: given this power imbalance, what is the safest way to connect?

cards.title: Partnership
cards.teaser: Two teams succeed or fail together. Partnership is the highest-trust relationship in the context map — both teams plan together, coordinate releases together, and share the cost of interface changes together.

runs.text: A
partnership

exists when two bounded contexts are jointly owned or so tightly aligned that one team cannot ship without coordinating with the other. There is no clear upstream/downstream — both teams share the cost of change. When one team changes an interface, the other team is involved from the design stage.
When it is appropriate:

items.text: Two teams building tightly coupled features on the same release timeline (e.g., a checkout context and a payments context launching a new payment method together).
Two contexts that will eventually be merged as the domain is understood better. Partnership acts as a temporary holding pattern while ownership is resolved.
Two teams so aligned in strategy that their separate ownership is primarily organizational, not technical.

runs.text: The costs of partnership:

items.text: High coordination overhead.
Both teams must align on release windows, API changes, and schema migrations. Neither can act unilaterally.
Shared failure mode.
If one team falls behind, the other is blocked. Partnership couples deployment velocity.
Difficult to sustain long-term.
As teams grow or organizational priorities diverge, partnerships tend to erode into customer-supplier or conformist relationships. Treat partnership as a temporary pattern, not a permanent one.

runs.text: Partnership is not the same as two teams sharing code in a monorepo. It requires an explicit mutual commitment to joint planning. Without that commitment, what looks like a partnership is usually a conformist relationship where one team silently dominates.
Partnership means neither team ships without checking with the other first. It is the highest trust and highest coordination cost of the eight patterns. Use it sparingly.

cards.title: Shared Kernel
cards.teaser: Two teams share a small, carefully defined slice of domain model — not the whole codebase, just the common core. High alignment on what belongs in the kernel is the price of entry. The coordination cost is real and ongoing.

runs.text: A
shared kernel

is a deliberate sharing of a subset of the domain model between two bounded contexts. Both contexts depend on the shared code. Neither team can change the shared kernel without coordinating with the other team. The shared portion is kept intentionally small — typically a set of value objects, domain events, or core identifiers that both contexts need to speak the same language.
A classic example: an e-commerce platform where the Order context and the Invoice context share a
Money
value object (currency, amount, rounding rules). Duplicating this type leads to subtle bugs when the two implementations diverge. Sharing a single canonical implementation prevents this.
Rules for a healthy shared kernel:

items.text: Define the kernel explicitly.
It lives in a named, versioned module or package — not in a shared utilities folder that accumulates everything nobody wants to own.
Keep it minimal.
Every type added to the kernel increases the coordination surface. If something can live in one context without causing duplication problems, keep it there.
Run both teams' test suites against it.
Any change to the kernel must pass tests from both dependent contexts before it can merge.
Treat changes as cross-team pull requests.
Both teams must review and approve changes. No unilateral modifications.

runs.text: A shared kernel that grows unchecked becomes a shared monolith. The moment teams start adding convenience code, business logic, or context-specific types to the kernel, it stops being a kernel and starts being a coupling problem. Audit its size at every sprint review.
A shared kernel is a small package of code two teams both use and both own. It stays small by design and only changes when both teams agree. If it grows, it turns into a coordination nightmare.

cards.title: Customer-Supplier
cards.teaser: The downstream team is the customer; the upstream team is the supplier. The customer has a voice — they can request features, file issues, and negotiate the interface. The supplier listens, but ultimately controls the roadmap.

runs.text: In a
customer-supplier

relationship, the upstream team acknowledges the downstream team as a legitimate stakeholder. There is an agreed-upon interface, and the downstream team has the ability to influence the upstream team's backlog — raise bugs, request new capabilities, and negotiate breaking changes. The upstream team may not always say yes, but they listen.

Real-world example: an internal platform team operating a data ingestion service. Three product teams consume it. The platform team maintains a backlog, holds regular office hours for the consumer teams, and provides a changelog and migration guide for any breaking changes. The product teams cannot merge into the platform codebase unilaterally, but they can (and do) file issues, propose interfaces, and escalate through management if the platform team is unresponsive.
Customer-supplier requires organizational backing:

items.text: The upstream team must have time allocated for customer-supplier responsibilities — roadmap alignment, API versioning, migration support.
Management must reinforce the pattern. If the upstream team ignores downstream requests with no consequence, the relationship collapses into conformist.
Acceptance tests owned by the downstream team validate the upstream contract. These are the downstream team's way of codifying their requirements as verifiable constraints.

runs.text: Customer-supplier is the ideal pattern for internal platform teams. It preserves upstream autonomy while giving downstream teams a structured way to influence the platform. It breaks down when one side is understaffed or when the relationship lacks management visibility.
Customer-supplier is like a business relationship: the supplier sets the product direction but genuinely listens to the customer. The customer can negotiate — they just cannot force a merge.

cards.title: Conformist
cards.teaser: The downstream team has no leverage. They consume the upstream model as-is, translate nothing, and absorb every breaking change. Conformism is not laziness — sometimes it is the rational choice when the upstream is large, stable, and not going to change for you.

runs.text: A
conformist

relationship exists when the downstream team decides to adopt the upstream model wholesale, without negotiation and without a translation layer. The downstream team simply uses the upstream's types, field names, concepts, and invariants directly in their own bounded context.
When conformism makes sense:

items.text: Consuming a well-designed, stable, industry-standard external API

where the upstream model is already the lingua franca of the domain (e.g., a startup building on top of Stripe for payments and simply using Stripe's PaymentIntent model directly without wrapping it).
A small downstream context with low complexity
where the overhead of an ACL exceeds the benefit. If the downstream context is a thin reporting layer, matching the upstream model is often the simplest approach.
When the upstream model aligns closely with the downstream domain
anyway. If the concepts map almost perfectly, conformism avoids the maintenance overhead of a translation layer that does almost nothing.

runs.text: The risk of conformism is conceptual contamination. Upstream concepts, field names, and data structures flow directly into the downstream model. If the upstream changes — or if the downstream domain evolves away from the upstream assumptions — the conformist context is tightly coupled and hard to refactor.

Conformism is often mistaken for pragmatism. Many systems that call themselves pragmatic are actually conformist contexts that grew too complex for the upstream model they absorbed. When a conformist context becomes large, the cost of rewriting it around its own domain model is very high. Make conformism explicit so the team knows they are making a deliberate coupling tradeoff.
Conformist means you use the upstream's model as your own. No translation, no negotiation. Simple — but you are stuck with whatever the upstream does, forever.

cards.title: Anticorruption Layer (ACL)
cards.teaser: An ACL is a translation layer that converts the upstream model into the downstream team's own language. The downstream context is insulated from upstream changes — when the upstream changes, only the ACL needs updating, not the entire downstream domain.

runs.text: The
anticorruption layer

(ACL) is the most important protective pattern in DDD. It sits at the boundary between two contexts and translates between their models. From the downstream context's perspective, the upstream model does not exist — only the downstream's own concepts exist. The ACL handles all mapping.
What an ACL typically contains:

items.text: Translators / mappers
— convert upstream DTOs or API responses into downstream domain objects. Field renames, type conversions, concept decompositions all live here.
Facades
— present a simplified interface to the downstream, hiding the complexity or inconsistency of the upstream API.
Adapters
— wrap the upstream transport (HTTP, gRPC, message queue) so the downstream domain does not know or care how the upstream is reached.

runs.text: Real-world example: a shipping context in an e-commerce company that integrates with FedEx's legacy SOAP API. FedEx uses concepts like
TrackingNumber
ServiceType
, and
ShipTimestamp
in their own idiosyncratic schema. The ACL translates these into
ShipmentId
DeliveryTier
, and
DispatchedAt
— the shipping context's own ubiquitous language. When FedEx upgrades to REST and renames their fields, only the ACL changes.

The ACL is the primary tool for integrating with external systems, legacy code, or any upstream context whose model you do not control and cannot improve. It is not overhead — it is the mechanism that prevents upstream entropy from spreading into the parts of your system you do control.
An ACL is a translation booth. Upstream speaks one language; downstream speaks another. The ACL sits in between, converting every message so each side only ever hears its own language.

cards.title: Open Host Service (OHS)
cards.teaser: An upstream context serving many downstream consumers formalizes its interface as an open protocol: documented, versioned, and stable. Instead of building custom integrations for each consumer, the upstream publishes one well-defined service that all consumers can use.

runs.text: An
open host service

(OHS) is the pattern an upstream context adopts when it has many downstream consumers. Rather than negotiating a custom integration contract with each consumer, the upstream team defines a formal, well-documented protocol that any authorized consumer can use without negotiation. The protocol becomes the product.

OHS shifts the integration burden from the upstream team to the downstream teams. The upstream no longer maintains N custom integrations; it maintains one protocol. Downstream teams that cannot work with the protocol must apply their own translation (typically via an ACL).
What makes an OHS different from just having an API:

items.text: Explicit versioning policy.
Consumers know which version they are using and how long it will be supported.
Stability guarantees.
The upstream team commits to a deprecation timeline. Changes are additive before they are breaking.
Designed for general use.
The API surface is designed for the general case, not for a specific consumer's needs. This requires more up-front design work than a custom integration.

runs.text: Real-world example:
Salesforce

operates as an OHS for hundreds of integration partners. They publish a documented REST API, a versioning scheme (v55.0, v56.0), a deprecation policy (3-year support window), and an SDK. No single consumer can negotiate a private protocol with Salesforce — they all use the published host service.

OHS is the pattern that internal platform teams should aspire to when their consumer count grows beyond two or three. A platform team that maintains custom integrations per consumer is not operating as an OHS — it is operating as a conformist supplier, and it will drown in coordination overhead.
OHS means the upstream team builds one door that everyone uses, instead of building a custom door for every person who wants to come in. The door is documented, versioned, and stable.

cards.title: Published Language
cards.teaser: A published language (PL) is a well-documented, shared information model — often an industry standard or an internal schema registry — that multiple contexts use to exchange data. It removes the need for point-to-point translation contracts between every pair of contexts.

runs.text: A
published language

(PL) is typically paired with an OHS. Where OHS describes the access mechanism (a versioned API), PL describes the shared information model that the API uses. It is the lingua franca of the integration: a schema, a set of domain events, or an information model that all contexts agree to speak.
Examples of published languages:

items.text: Industry standards:
HL7 FHIR for healthcare data exchange. FIX protocol for financial instruments. ACORD for insurance. These are published languages — every system in the domain speaks them.
Internal event schemas:

A company's internal Avro or Protobuf schemas for domain events published to Kafka. The schema registry is the PL. Every producer and consumer agrees on the schema. Adding a field is a breaking change that must be versioned.
GraphQL schema as PL:
A company's federated GraphQL schema that multiple front-end contexts query. The schema is the published language; the federation gateway is the OHS.

runs.text: When PL and OHS are used together, the context map shows them as a combined label. A downstream context that cannot map its own domain to the published language still needs an ACL — the PL does not eliminate the need for translation within the downstream context; it just reduces the surface area of translation to the gap between the PL and the downstream model.

A published language is most powerful when it models the problem domain, not an implementation artifact. HL7 FHIR works because it models clinical care concepts, not hospital software data structures. Design PL around stable domain concepts, not current database schemas.

A published language is the shared dictionary everyone in the room agreed to use before the meeting started. Once it exists, everyone translates to it — you do not need a separate translator for every pair of speakers.

cards.title: Separate Ways
cards.teaser: Sometimes the best integration strategy is no integration at all. Two contexts that share no meaningful domain concepts are better off developing independently than paying the coordination cost of a formal relationship.

runs.text: The pattern
Separate ways

exists when two bounded contexts have no meaningful relationship worth formalizing. Each team goes their own way. There is no shared model, no formal integration, and no coordination overhead. If the two contexts ever need to exchange data, they do it through an export/import mechanism (files, reports, batch jobs) rather than a real-time integration.
When separate ways is correct:

items.text: The contexts operate in genuinely different sub-domains with no shared entities.
A legal document management context and a machine learning experimentation platform in the same company may have no meaningful domain overlap.
The integration cost exceeds the integration value.
Sometimes two contexts could share data, but the volume, frequency, and criticality of that sharing does not justify building and maintaining an integration.
The integration would force model pollution.
If integrating two contexts requires one or both to adopt concepts that do not belong in their domain, separate ways protects model integrity.

runs.text: Separate ways appears on a context map as two isolated boxes with no arrows between them. This explicit representation matters: it signals that the separation is intentional, not accidental neglect. Teams that do not draw a context map often accidentally implement conformist relationships where separate ways would have been better.

A context map with no separate ways relationships is a warning sign. In large organizations, not every context needs to integrate with every other context. If every box on your map has arrows to every other box, the map is showing coupling, not architecture.

Sometimes the right answer is: these two teams have nothing useful to say to each other. Separate ways means no integration, no shared model, no coordination. Explicitly choosing this is a valid architectural decision.

cards.title: Big Ball of Mud
cards.teaser: A big ball of mud is what you get when there is no bounded context. Everything knows about everything, models leak everywhere, and no team owns anything. It is not an integration pattern — it is the absence of integration patterns.

runs.text: Brian Foote and Joseph Yoder named the
big ball of mud

in their 1997 paper of the same name. Evans adopted it into DDD as the canonical anti-pattern — the outcome of a system that grew without bounded contexts, context maps, or deliberate integration patterns.
Recognizing a big ball of mud on a context map:

items.text: The system cannot be decomposed into contexts.
Every change requires touching code in multiple logical areas because nothing is encapsulated.
No team fully owns any part.
Responsibility is diffuse. No one can authorize a change to a given piece of code with confidence.
Domain language is inconsistent.
The same concept is called
user
in one module,
account
in another, and
customer
in a third. These are not synonyms — they reflect different models that were never reconciled.
Integration points are undocumented.
There is no context map because there are no contexts. A change to the database schema breaks ten things because all ten things share the schema without an integration layer.

runs.text: Drawing the big ball of mud on a context map does not mean accepting it. It means naming it honestly so that the team can decide which parts to extract first and which patterns to apply to each extraction. Most real systems have at least one big ball of mud region.

Include the big ball of mud explicitly on the context map. Teams that pretend it does not exist draw maps that show only the clean parts of the system — and then wonder why their migration plans fail when they encounter the parts that were left off the map.
A big ball of mud is what you get when nobody ever drew a boundary. Everything depends on everything. The context map has no clean boxes — just one big smear. You name it to fix it, not to accept it.

cards.title: Modernizing Legacy Systems via ACL: The Strangler-Fig Connection
cards.teaser: The anticorruption layer is the enabling mechanism for the strangler-fig pattern. New bounded contexts grow around a legacy big ball of mud, each protected by an ACL. Over time, the new contexts absorb the legacy's responsibilities and the old system is decommissioned.

runs.text: Martin Fowler's
strangler-fig application

pattern describes a migration strategy: build new functionality alongside the legacy system, gradually routing traffic to the new system until the legacy can be safely decommissioned — like a strangler fig vine that grows around a tree until the tree is no longer needed.

The ACL is what makes this possible in practice. Without it, the new bounded context would need to use the legacy system's model directly — contaminating the new domain from day one and making it harder, not easier, to eventually remove the legacy.
The strangler-fig migration sequence using an ACL:

items.text: Step 1: Draw the context map.
Identify which capabilities of the big ball of mud are candidates for extraction. Name the target bounded contexts you want to grow.
Step 2: Build the ACL at the legacy boundary.
The ACL translates between the legacy's data model and the new context's model. The new context never imports from the legacy system directly.
Step 3: Route new traffic to the new context.
New features and new data paths go through the new bounded context. The legacy handles only existing flows.
Step 4: Incrementally migrate existing flows.
Move legacy responsibilities into the new context piece by piece. The ACL handles backward compatibility during the transition.
Step 5: Decommission.
When all traffic has moved to the new contexts, the legacy system is removed. The ACL is also removed or reduced to a thin shim for any remaining external integrations.

runs.text: The most common failure mode of legacy modernization is skipping the ACL and letting the new system absorb the legacy model. The new system then contains a big ball of mud from day one, the migration cost doubles, and the project is often cancelled mid-way. The ACL overhead in the short term is the price of a successful long-term migration.

The ACL is how you build a new house next to the old one without the old house's floor plan dictating the new house's layout. The ACL handles the translation between the two until you are ready to tear the old one down.

cards.title: All Eight Patterns: A Comparison Table
cards.teaser: The eight context-map patterns differ on three axes: the level of team autonomy, the degree of model coupling, and the coordination cost. Choosing the right pattern is as much an organizational decision as a technical one.

runs.text: A side-by-side comparison of all eight relationship patterns:

items.text: Partnership:
No clear U/D. Both teams plan together. Highest coordination cost. Use for tightly coupled features on the same release train.
Shared Kernel:
Shared small model subset. Both teams own the kernel. High coupling within the kernel; autonomy outside it. Use when two contexts share unavoidable concepts.
Customer-Supplier:
Clear U/D. Downstream has a voice. Medium coordination cost. Use for internal platform-consumer relationships.
Conformist:
Clear U/D. Downstream has no voice. Low coordination cost, high coupling. Use when upstream model is stable and the downstream is simple.
Anticorruption Layer:
Clear U/D. Downstream is fully protected. Medium implementation cost; low ongoing coupling. Use when downstream model must be kept clean from upstream changes.
Open Host Service:
Clear U/D. Upstream serves many downstreams with one protocol. Low per-consumer coordination cost. Use when one context must serve many consumers.
Published Language:
Paired with OHS. Shared information model. Enables multi-context integration via a common schema. Use alongside OHS in high-fanout scenarios.
Separate Ways:
No relationship. Zero coordination cost. Zero integration. Use when two contexts share no meaningful domain overlap.

runs.text: The progression from Partnership through Conformist represents decreasing mutual commitment between teams. The progression from Conformist through ACL represents increasing downstream investment in protecting their own model. OHS/PL represents the upstream investment in serving many consumers cleanly.

Most real systems use multiple patterns simultaneously. The same company might have Partnership between two co-owned contexts, Customer-Supplier with an internal platform, ACL against a legacy ERP, and Conformist consumption of Stripe. The context map shows all of them together.

Eight patterns, one question: given this power dynamic and this domain relationship, what is the right way to connect? The answer is always a point on the spectrum from full shared ownership (partnership) to complete independence (separate ways).

cards.title: When to Choose Which Pattern
cards.teaser: Pattern selection is driven by three factors: team power dynamics, how much the downstream model must be protected, and the number of consumers. Getting the selection wrong produces either over-coordination or hidden coupling.

runs.text: A practical decision tree for choosing an integration pattern:

items.text: Is the upstream external and unchangeable?
(SaaS, third-party API, legacy with no owner) → If yes: use
ACL
unless the upstream model maps cleanly to your domain, in which case
Conformist
is acceptable for small, low-complexity contexts.
Does the upstream serve many consumers?
→ Upstream should adopt
OHS + Published Language
. Each downstream decides independently whether to be Conformist (use the PL directly) or to add an ACL (translate the PL into their own model).
Is the downstream team able to influence the upstream backlog?
→ Yes:
Customer-Supplier
. No: Conformist or ACL depending on model compatibility.
Do both teams share a release and failure fate?
Partnership
(temporary). Plan to evolve toward Customer-Supplier as team autonomy increases.
Do the two contexts share unavoidable core concepts?
Shared Kernel
for that minimum subset. All other integration uses separate patterns.
Do the two contexts have no meaningful domain overlap?
Separate Ways
. Document the decision explicitly on the context map.

runs.text: The most common mistake: applying Conformist where ACL is needed because the ACL feels like over-engineering on day one. The test is not complexity today — it is the anticipated rate of upstream change and the criticality of the downstream model's integrity.

Revisit the context map when organizational structure changes. Team merges, acquisitions, and reorgs change the power dynamics that drive pattern selection. A Customer-Supplier that made sense with two separate teams becomes Partnership — or degenerates into Conformist — when the teams merge or one is dissolved.

The right pattern depends on who controls the model, how many consumers there are, and how much the downstream needs to protect its own language. Answer those three questions and the right pattern becomes obvious.
